pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 11–12: extend the order of operations to include POWERS, ROOTS and RECIPROCALS — use conventional priority notation (BIDMAS/BODMAS) to evaluate complex numerical expressions, and understand a number times its reciprocal is 1.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): 'use conventional notation for priority of operations, including brackets, powers, roots and reciprocals'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 6.EE.1 (write and evaluate numerical expressions involving whole-number exponents); the precedence of exponents within order of operations is formalised in Grade 6.
• Operational details — insert the Indices/Orders tier between Brackets and ×÷: Brackets → Indices (powers & roots) → ×÷ (L→R) → +− (L→R). Evaluate expressions like 3 + 2³ × 4 or √(9+16). Introduce the reciprocal (1/n) as the multiplicative inverse — n × 1/n = 1 — and note division by n equals multiplication by its reciprocal. Reinforce that the whole convention is an agreed anti-ambiguity notation, extended, not a new rule set.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 11): evaluate an expression with one power correctly (3 + 2³×4 = 35). Tier B (11–12): evaluate an expression mixing brackets, a root/power and all four operations. Tier C (12): explain why order of operations avoids ambiguity, and use a reciprocal (n × 1/n = 1; ÷n = ×1/n).
bestPractices: Slot the new INDICES tier explicitly into the already-secured Y6 hierarchy (prerequisite mt_jHgRQ4hR0g): powers and roots sit just below brackets and above ×÷ — present it as an extension of a known ladder, not a fresh acronym.
Keep reinforcing that ×÷ share a tier and +− share a tier (swept L→R); the BIDMAS acronym still misleads on D-before-M and A-before-S, so rehearse counterexamples with powers added.
Teach the reciprocal via the defining property n × 1/n = 1 and connect ÷n = ×1/n — seeding fraction division and later algebra; use it to show why reciprocals are 'undo by multiply'.
Confront power-specific traps directly: 2³ means 2×2×2 = 8 (not 2×3 = 6), and −3² vs (−3)² differ because the power binds tighter than the negative sign unless bracketed.
Motivate with genuine ambiguity: show a calculator or two people disagreeing on 3 + 2³ × 4, then resolve with the extended hierarchy, so the convention is felt as necessary.
keyRepresentations: Extended hierarchy ladder with the new Indices step inserted between Brackets and ×÷.
Colour-tiered annotation of an expression (brackets, then powers/roots, then ×÷, then +−) before evaluation.
Reciprocal pairing: n and 1/n shown multiplying to 1 (e.g. on a number line or as a product returning to unity).
Step-by-step rewrite chain collapsing one tier per line (3 + 2³×4 → 3 + 8×4 → 3 + 32 → 35).
commonMisconceptions: Evaluating powers as multiplication: 2³ = 6 instead of 8.
Applying the acronym literally — doing division before multiplication or addition before subtraction because I/D/A appear first.
Mishandling sign vs power: −3² taken as (−3)² = 9 rather than −(3²) = −9.
Thinking the reciprocal of n is −n (confusing multiplicative inverse with additive inverse) rather than 1/n.
Treating roots as outside the hierarchy, or evaluating under a root before resolving the bracket-like grouping the root implies (√(9+16) ≠ √9 + √16).

learn.summary: For ages 11–12: extend the order of operations to include an Indices tier (powers and roots) sitting between brackets and ×÷, and introduce the reciprocal as the multiplicative inverse (n × 1/n = 1, with ÷n = ×1/n). Learners evaluate complex expressions tier by tier, confront power-specific traps (2³ ≠ 2×3; −3² vs (−3)²; a root sign implies grouping), and grasp that the whole convention is an agreed anti-ambiguity notation, not an arbitrary rule. Activities range from a live expression-resolving tool (primary proposal) through anchor charts, consolidation questions, and Socratic justification.

activities.title: Resolve the expression one tier at a time
feedback: If a learner gives 2³ = 6, write 2×2×2 and count the factors: the exponent says how many copies of the base are multiplied together, not what to multiply the base by.
If a learner evaluates √9 + √16 = 7, point to the grouping the root sign implies: resolve 9+16 = 25 first, then √25 = 5.

If a learner adds before multiplying (power resolved to 2³ = 8, then 3 + 8 = 11, ×4 = 44), replay both orders side by side so the diverging answers (44 vs 35) show why multiplication is resolved before addition; separately, if a learner misreads the power itself (e.g. 2³ read as 2×3 = 6), handle that as the power-meaning error above.

Optional live supports that make the mechanism concrete: a tier-highlighter that shades each band as it is resolved; a step-by-step rewrite chain collapsing one tier per line; a tool that refuses the mis-ordered path and plays out both answers for comparison. These are illustrative, not required.
activities.rationale: Order of operations with an added tier is structural and sequential; resolving an expression step by step, including a deliberate wrong-order comparison, targets the common error of treating the acronym as a literal sequence and of mishandling powers and roots. KS3 names powers and roots within priority notation and Grade 6 formalises the precedence of exponents.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils use conventional notation for the priority of operations, including brackets, powers, roots and reciprocals.
Grade 6 pupils write and evaluate numerical expressions involving whole-number exponents, formalising the precedence of exponents within the order of operations.
learnerActions: Work with a live expression such as 3 + 2³ × 4 and decide which operation to resolve next, following the hierarchy Brackets → Indices (powers & roots) → ×÷ (left to right) → +− (left to right).
Resolve the power first: 2³ = 8 (write out 2×2×2 to confirm it is not 2×3 = 6), then ×4 = 32, then +3 = 35.
Deliberately try the wrong order — doing the addition before the multiplication: 3 + 2³ = 11, then × 4 = 44 — and compare 44 with the correct 35 so the two answers are seen to diverge.
Annotate an expression by shading each tier a different colour (brackets, then powers/roots, then ×÷, then +−) before collapsing it one tier per line: 3 + 2³×4 → 3 + 8×4 → 3 + 32 → 35.
Evaluate √(9+16): resolve the grouping under the root first (9+16 = 25) then take √25 = 5, and check that this is not √9 + √16 = 3+4 = 7.
activities.intendedInsight: Indices (powers and roots) rank just below brackets and above ×÷; evaluating in the agreed order produces one unambiguous value, and a root implies grouping of what sits under it.

activities.title: The sign-versus-power boundary: −3² vs (−3)²
feedback: If a learner says −3² = 9, show that the exponent attaches to the 3 only: −3² reads as the negative of 3², i.e. −(9) = −9.
If a learner treats (−3)² as −9, point out the bracket groups the minus with the 3 so both factors are negative, giving +9.
An optional toggle that drops a bracket in and shows the answer flip 9 ↔ −9 makes the boundary vivid; a fixed worked pair of both cases also teaches it.
activities.rationale: The −3² vs (−3)² confusion is a named misconception; making the bracket's effect explicit addresses it directly without claiming a single medium is required.
learnerActions: Evaluate −3² by noting the power binds tighter than the negative sign: −3² = −(3²) = −9.
Evaluate (−3)² where the bracket groups the negative with the base: (−3)² = (−3)×(−3) = 9.
Add or remove a bracket around a negative number and predict how the value flips between −9 and 9 before confirming.
activities.intendedInsight: Without brackets, a power applies only to the number immediately beneath it, not to a preceding minus sign; bracketing changes what the exponent acts on.

activities.title: Reciprocals as multiplicative inverse
feedback: If a learner says the reciprocal of n is −n, check the defining property: n × (−n) is not 1, but n × 1/n = 1.
If a learner cannot link reciprocals to division, show ÷n and ×1/n acting on the same number and compare the results.

An optional reciprocal station where a number is dragged onto its ×1/n partner and the product settles to 1, with a ÷n swapped for ×1/n to see them land identically, makes the inverse relationship observable; a number line showing n and 1/n multiplying to unity works similarly.
activities.rationale: Teaching the reciprocal via its defining property seeds fraction division and later algebra and counters the additive-vs-multiplicative inverse confusion. KS3 priority notation explicitly includes reciprocals.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils use conventional notation for the priority of operations, including brackets, powers, roots and reciprocals.
learnerActions: State the reciprocal of a non-zero number n as 1/n and multiply n × 1/n, confirming the product is exactly 1 (e.g. 5 × 1/5 = 1); note that 0 has no reciprocal.
Compare dividing by n with multiplying by 1/n on the same number, checking the two operations give the same result (÷n = ×1/n).
Distinguish the reciprocal (multiplicative inverse, 1/n) from the negative (additive inverse, −n): the reciprocal of 5 is 1/5, not −5.
Match each number to its reciprocal (e.g. 4 ↔ 1/4, 2/3 ↔ 3/2).
activities.intendedInsight: Any non-zero number times its reciprocal is 1, so the reciprocal is what you multiply by to 'undo' multiplication, and dividing by a non-zero number is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal (0 has no reciprocal).

activities.title: Why do we need an agreed order? (justify the convention)
feedback: If a learner says 'that's just the rule', show the same expression producing two answers under two orders and ask which one others should read it as.
Accept any explanation that captures the idea that shared notation must yield one value to be useful for communicating calculations.
activities.rationale: The conceptual heart of this topic is ambiguity-removal; a discussion or Socratic prompt supports justification, which procedural practice alone may leave implicit. This is complementary to the hands-on evaluation, not a substitute for it.
learnerActions: Take a single expression such as 3 + 2³ × 4 and compute it under two different orders, recording the two different values (e.g. 35 vs 44).
Explain in your own words why mathematicians need one agreed order: so the same written expression communicates a single unambiguous value.
Respond to a prompt that offers two conflicting values and justify which order and result is correct and why.
activities.intendedInsight: The order of operations exists to remove ambiguity so notation communicates one value, not because any single order is inherently 'more correct'.

activities.title: Consolidation check
feedback: For 3 + 2³ × 4, flag 44 as the 'added before multiplying' error (power resolved to 8, then 3 + 8 = 11, ×4 = 44) and any value using 2³ = 6; confirm 35 with the tier order.
For √(9+16) + 2×5, check the learner resolved the grouping under the root (25 → 5) before combining with 2×5 = 10, giving 15.
activities.rationale: Short checks consolidate and surface residual errors (adding first, exponent-as-multiplier, sign/power). Recognition and matching test outcomes rather than building the structural insight, so use them after the construction activities.
learnerActions: Evaluate 3 + 2³ × 4 and justify why 35 is correct (not 44 from adding before multiplying, and not using 2³ = 6).
Decide whether −3² equals −9 or 9 and explain the bracket rule.
Match numbers to their reciprocals and state what each pair multiplies to.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can evaluate expressions with the new tier correctly and articulate the reciprocal relationship under assessment conditions.

constraints: Present the Indices tier as an extension of the already-secured brackets→×÷→+− hierarchy, not a brand-new acronym.

Keep reinforcing that ×÷ share one tier and +− share one tier, both swept left to right; BIDMAS/BODMAS still misleads on division-before-multiplication and addition-before-subtraction even with indices added — rehearse counterexamples.
A root sign implies grouping of what sits beneath it: resolve under the root before taking the root (√(9+16) = √25 = 5, not √9 + √16 = 7).

Recognition/matching and multiple-choice checks assess outcomes but do not by themselves build the structural, step-by-step insight; pair them with activities where learners resolve expressions and witness the reciprocal returning to 1.

Optional interactive supports (tier-highlighter, wrong-path comparison, drag-to-reciprocal station) make mechanisms concrete but are illustrative examples, not required mechanisms; the same ideas can be taught on paper or with worked pairs.
A fixed worked example cannot be manipulated live but can still teach the −3² vs (−3)² and reciprocal relationships.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and no empirical effectiveness is claimed.

The 44 value is the intended wrong-order result for 3 + 2³ × 4, reached by resolving the power first (2³=8) and then adding before multiplying (3+8=11, ×4=44). It demonstrates that multiplication precedes addition, and is used only as a flagged error, never as a correct option.

Audit of the original assessment: the diagnostic prompt 'Evaluate 2 + 3 × 4²' has correctAnswer 50 (4²=16, 3×16=48, 2+48=50) — arithmetically correct, and the probeDeeper question 'Why did you work out 4² before multiplying by 3?' is consistent with it.

The assessment distractor '2 + (3×4)² = 146' is arithmetically correct ((12)²=144, +2=146) and is a valid wrong-order distractor; used conceptually in consolidation without presenting it as a correct answer.
The source claim that BIDMAS/BODMAS misleads on D-before-M and A-before-S is NCETM-attributed guidance (verified:false in the row); preserved in constraints but not cited as established efficacy.
The parentTitle 'Ratio (age 11+)' appears inconsistent with the order-of-operations/reciprocals content; flagged as a possible source mislabel, not resolved here.

probeDeeper: Why did you work out 4² before multiplying by 3?
What would this expression equal if we just went left to right — and why is that not allowed?
Why do mathematicians need an agreed order at all?
What is the reciprocal of 5, and what do you get when you multiply 5 by it?
assess.correctAnswer: 50 (indices first: 4² = 16; then multiply: 3 × 16 = 48; then add: 2 + 48 = 50). The reason tier: without an agreed order the same expression would give different answers for different people, so the notation would be ambiguous and useless for communicating calculations.

errorPatterns.pattern: handles indices in the wrong place — multiplies 3×4 before squaring, or squares the product (3×4)²
errorPatterns.nextMove: place indices just after brackets in the priority; 4² binds tighter than the multiplication — evaluate the power before combining.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer such as 2 + 12² or (3×4)²-based value; power not evaluated first

errorPatterns.pattern: reads the exponent as a multiplier — 4² as 4×2 = 8
errorPatterns.nextMove: 4² means 4×4; distinguish the exponent (how many factors) from a multiplier.

errorPatterns.pattern: sees order-of-operations as an arbitrary rule with no purpose — cannot say why agreement matters
errorPatterns.nextMove: show the SAME expression giving two different answers under two orders; the convention exists so notation communicates one unambiguous value.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: on the reason tier the child says 'that's just the rule' with no notion of ambiguity

errorPatterns.pattern: does not connect reciprocals to division — unsure that a × (1/a) = 1
errorPatterns.nextMove: define the reciprocal as the number you multiply by to get 1; ×(1/a) undoes ×a, linking to inverse operations.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: when asked, cannot state that a number times its reciprocal is 1

responseLevels.gap: mis-orders indices or reads the exponent as a multiplier; sees the convention as purposeless.
responseLevels.full: evaluates brackets/indices/operations in correct priority, justifies the convention as removing ambiguity, and understands reciprocals as multiplicative inverses giving 1.
responseLevels.partial: evaluates the expression correctly but explains the order only as 'the rule', without the ambiguity rationale; shaky on reciprocals.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Evaluate 2 + 3 × 4². Then tell me: why must everyone agree on an order for working this out — what would go wrong if they didn't?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Adding indices to the mix is where children who 'know BODMAS' as a word but not as a priority reveal gaps — they may do the multiplication before the power, or add first. The reason tier tests whether they grasp that order-of-operations exists to remove AMBIGUITY, the conceptual heart, not just a mnemonic.
